title: Gratitude for the ordinary
hookLine: the people who taught you without a title

lines: A BROOM BY THE MOSQUE DOOR.
THE GRANDMOTHER, THE NEIGHBOR, THE FRIEND.
cards: A broom leans against the wall by the door of a mosque. Somebody uses it every evening after the last prayer, and nobody thinks to ask who. Yesterday was for the scholars with names on book spines.
Today is for the others. The grandmother who said bismillah before every bite until it stuck. The neighbor who showed a nervous kid where to put their shoes.
The friend who answered a clumsy question about Ramadan without making anyone feel foolish. None of them had a title. Some taught more than any book.

teach.h: THANK PEOPLE, AND YOU'VE THANKED GOD.
teach.b: First, thanking people is part of thanking God. In a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah.
Gratitude that skips the person in front of you isn't finished.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO SWEPT THE MOSQUE.
teach.b: Second, the one who swept the mosque. In Sahih al-Bukhari there's a report about a Black woman, or a man, the narrator wasn't sure which, who used to sweep the mosque.
One day the Prophet noticed she was gone and asked about her. She had died, and no one had told him. In Sahih Muslim's telling, people thought it a small matter.
He said, in paraphrase: why didn't you tell me? Show me her grave. He went and prayed at her grave.
Nobody had thought her worth a message. He thought her worth a visit.
Third, the first teachers of all. The Qur'an asks for thanks to Allah and to one's parents in one breath.

And it gives a line to say for them, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little." Care when you were little is teaching too, the kind no one writes down.
Fourth, the untitled teachers now. The aunt who corrected a verse gently. The coworker who covered a shift so someone could make Friday prayer.
The stranger in a mosque who lent a prayer mat and said nothing.
The hadith puts thanks to them inside thanks to Allah, and the Prophet's walk to a grave shows the honor doesn't end when they do.

how: Muslims say jazakallahu khayran, may Allah reward you with good, to thank someone, and in some families children learn the first words of the faith at home, long before any class.

games.q: what does “gratitude for the ordinary” mean?
o: thanks owed to people with no title who taught you by doing
a smaller kind of thanks than what we owe to scholars
thanks owed to God alone, never to the people around you

games.q: gratitude for the ordinary — tap the pairs.
p: the one who swept the mosque
the Prophet asked to see her grave
thanks to Allah and to parents
asked for together in the Qur'an
as they did care for me when I was little

s: gratitude to God and gratitude to people are separate matters
the hadith in Abu Dawud ties them: whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah.
the Prophet went to the grave of the one who swept the mosque
in Sahih al-Bukhari, he asked to be shown the grave and prayed there.
the people thought it right to tell the Prophet she had died
they thought it a small matter and didn't tell him; he asked why.

games.q: the Prophet asks after the one who swept the mosque. people say she died, and they didn't think it worth telling him. what does he do?
o: says nothing; it was a small matter.
asks to be shown the grave, and prays there.
asks who will sweep the mosque now.
games.why: in Sahih al-Bukhari he asks why they didn't tell him, has them show him the grave, and prays for her.

practice: Let one face come to mind, someone who taught you something about faith, or about being a decent person, and never got called a teacher for it. Remember the moment, and shape one sentence of thanks you could give them.
If they have died, and if you pray, you can say the Qur'an's line for parents, or simply ask mercy for them.

wordCard.voice: Gratitude for the ordinary. Thanks owed to the people with no title who taught by doing, because thanking them is part of thanking God. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: thanks, gratitude; the opposite in the Qur'an is kufr, ingratitude.

carryVoice: Your line: untitled teachers. Some of the best teaching never came with a title. Go gently.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 4811 (whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 458 (the one who swept the mosque; the Prophet prays at the grave)
Sahih Muslim 956 (they thought her matter small; he prayed at the grave)
Qur'an 31:14 (give thanks to Me and to your parents)

sources.q: My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little.
